analysis.one_liner: Doubles the research tax credit rate and lets more startups claim it against payroll taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on July 23, 2020, received no committee action or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill doubles the main research tax credit, from 20% to 40% of qualifying research spending, and doubles the alternative simplified credit from 14% to 28%. It also makes it easier for small startup companies to use the credit: it raises the cap on claiming the credit against payroll taxes from $250,000 to $500,000 per year and broadens which small businesses qualify. The changes take effect for tax years after 2019 and 2020 and include no offsetting revenue. The bill never moved past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that spend heavily on research and development — including large tech, pharmaceutical, and manufacturing firms — would pay less in federal taxes under the doubled credit rates. Startup companies with revenue under the small-business threshold would gain the ability to claim up to $500,000 per year of the credit against payroll taxes, which matters for young firms that owe no income tax yet but have employees [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the standard research credit rate from 20% to 40% of qualifying research spending, and the alternative simplified credit from 14% to 28% [S2] [S3].

Raises the annual cap on using the credit against payroll taxes from $250,000 to $500,000 for eligible small businesses, and ties the gross-receipts eligibility threshold to the inflation-adjusted small-business definition in section 448(c)(1) instead of a fixed $5 million [S2] [S3].
For young companies that owe no income tax, the payroll-tax offset converts the credit into cash that can offset the employer share of payroll taxes, easing cash flow in the earliest years [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers as a whole, through reduced federal revenue. Doubling the credit rates has no offsetting tax increase or spending cut in the bill, so the cost is added to the deficit [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no offsetting revenue, so doubling the credit rates would increase the federal deficit, and the benefit flows mostly to companies that were already spending on research and would likely do some of that research anyway [S3].

The research credit has long been criticized as a reward for spending companies would undertake regardless, meaning a large share of the doubled credit is a pure tax cut rather than new innovation [S3].
The largest dollar value of the doubled rates goes to the biggest R&D spenders — large tech and pharmaceutical firms — not to the small startups the bill's title emphasizes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The startup provisions have a plausible case: letting young firms use the credit against payroll taxes addresses a real problem, since a company losing money gets no benefit from an income-tax credit. But the bill's centerpiece — doubling every research credit rate with no pay-for — is a broad tax cut whose benefits scale with how much research a company already spends, which concentrates the gains in the largest corporations. An honest supporter would acknowledge that much of the doubled credit subsidizes spending that would have happened anyway, at a cost carried by all taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or markup, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jackie Walorski introduced the bill on July 23, 2020, joined by Rep. Jodey Arrington, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means and to its Subcommittee on Select Revenue Measures [S1] [S3] [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No constituency won a change; the outcome preserved the status quo. Taxpayers avoided the cost of a doubled, unpaid-for corporate credit, while R&D-heavy companies kept the existing 20% rate rather than gaining the doubled one.

for.name: Rep. Jackie Walorski
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means member

for.name: Rep. Jodey Arrington
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as an original cosponsor.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup; no committee action was recorded after referral.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Republican — the sponsor and both cosponsors were House Republicans, and the committee chaired by a Democrat took no action on the bill [S1] [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Doubling the credit rates from 20% to 40% would roughly double the value of an existing tax benefit that scales with research spending, so the largest R&D budgets capture the most money. Because the bill has no offset, the cost lands on federal taxpayers [S3].

Raising the payroll-tax offset cap to $500,000 and broadening eligibility lets cash-strapped young firms turn the credit into money that offsets payroll taxes — a genuine cash-flow benefit for companies with no income-tax liability yet [S2] [S3].
